examples.problem_statement:
Select the two answer choices that, when used to complete the sentence, fit the meaning of the sentence as a whole and produce completed sentences that are alike in meaning.

Skeptics contend that any scheme for charging visitors to Web sites that rewards the vendor adequately would require steep prices, ______ the kind of frequent, casual use of Web sites that surfers now take for granted.

A bridling  B exciting  C forbidding  D inhibiting  E provoking  F reversing

solution.operation: Read the sentence as skeptics' reaction to a plan that raises revenue by charging visitors to Web sites
solution.result: The blank must describe the effect of "steep prices" on frequent, casual use
solution.description: Fix what the sentence is about before touching the choices: the skeptics' objection is what the blank has to justify.

solution.operation: Translate the skeptics' objection into a required direction for the blank: steep prices must be associated with a decrease in visitor volume
solution.result: The blank needs a word meaning "holds back / cuts down" casual use
solution.description: Convert the logic of the sentence into an explicit requirement, so each choice can be tested against one fixed criterion.

solution.operation: Scan the six choices for a PAIR that both mean "holds back" and are alike in meaning as completed sentences
solution.result: "bridling" and "inhibiting" are the only two consistent with the logic and nearly alike in meaning
solution.description: Sentence Equivalence needs two choices, so look for a matching pair rather than a single best word.

solution.operation: Reject "forbidding" as too strong for the required decrease
solution.result: "forbidding" eliminated: steep prices might dissuade a casual visitor, but they would not forbid one
solution.description: Test the tempting near-miss: it points the right direction but overshoots the strength the sentence supports.

solution.operation: Reject "exciting" and "provoking", the other similar-meaning pair
solution.result: "exciting" and "provoking" eliminated: they can be similar in meaning but do not fit the logic of the sentence
solution.description: Confirm that forming a synonym pair is not sufficient; the pair must also satisfy the direction fixed in step 2.

examples.answer: Choice A: bridling AND Choice D: inhibiting

key_reminders: The two chosen words must both fit the sentence's logic AND yield completed sentences alike in meaning.
A word pointing the right direction can still be wrong if its strength exceeds what the sentence supports.
A synonym pair that contradicts the sentence's logic is a trap, not an answer.
common_mistakes: Picking the synonym pair "exciting"/"provoking" because they match each other, ignoring that steep prices reduce rather than spur casual use.
Choosing "forbidding" for its strong negative force when the sentence only supports discouragement.

examples.problem_statement:
Select the two answer choices that, when used to complete the sentence, fit the meaning of the sentence as a whole and produce completed sentences that are alike in meaning.

Some analysts worry about consumers' perception that the electronics industry is always on the verge of major breakthroughs; that perception could hurt the industry by making consumers reluctant to buy products they believe will soon be ______ .

A incompatible  B devalued  C obsolete  D ubiquitous  E everywhere  F outmoded

solution.operation: Characterize the blank from the sentence: it describes products consumers fear will be superseded in quality because of coming breakthroughs
solution.result: The blank needs a word meaning "superseded / out of date"
solution.description: Derive the required meaning from the clause about breakthroughs before looking at the options.

solution.operation: Test the pair "ubiquitous" and "everywhere" against that requirement
solution.result: Rejected: they produce sentences with the same meaning but assume an increase in volume or sales, which innovatory breakthroughs do not necessarily imply
solution.description: Check the obvious synonym pair; matching each other is not enough if the meaning is not the one the sentence calls for.

solution.operation: Test "devalued" for a partner among the remaining choices
solution.result: Rejected: it makes a coherent sentence, but no other choice would produce a sentence with the same meaning
solution.description: Apply the two-answer constraint: a word that works alone is unusable if it has no equivalent partner in the list.

solution.operation: Select "obsolete" and "outmoded" as the pair meaning superseded
solution.result: Both fit the fear of being superseded and give sentences alike in meaning
solution.description: Commit to the pair that satisfies both requirements at once: correct meaning and equivalence to each other.

examples.answer: Choice C: obsolete; AND Choice F: outmoded

key_reminders: Both answers must fit the sentence AND produce completed sentences alike in meaning.
A choice with no meaning-partner among the options cannot be part of the answer, however sensible it sounds alone.
A synonym pair must still match the specific idea the sentence sets up.
common_mistakes: Selecting "ubiquitous"/"everywhere" because they are exact synonyms, though the sentence is about products being superseded, not about their spread.
Keeping "devalued" as one answer when nothing in the list pairs with it in meaning.

examples.problem_statement:
World Bank. In 2010, China comprised about 10 percent of the world's gross domestic product (GDP), and its voting share in the World Bank was increased from less than 3 percent to 4.4 percent. During the same time frame, France comprised about 4 percent of the world's GDP and saw its voting share in the World bank drop from 4.3 percent to 3.8 percent.
Which of the following can be logically concluded from the passage above?

(A) Prior to 2010, China comprised less than 10 percent of the world's GDP.
(B) Voting share in the World Bank is not directly proportional to each country's share of the world's GDP.
(C) China's share in the world's GDP is increasing more rapidly than France's share.
(D) The Chinese government is likely to be dissatisfied with the degree of the increase in its voting share.
(E) World Bank voting shares are allocated based upon each country's share of the world's gross domestic product during previous years, not during the present year.

solution.operation: Read the question stem for its task language: "can be logically concluded from the passage above"
solution.result: Identified as an Inference question
solution.description: Classify the question first, because the wording "logically concluded" sets the standard the right answer must meet.

solution.operation: Map the China numbers: 2010, China GDP 10, vote share less than 3 raised to 4.4
solution.result: China: GDP about 10 percent; vote share <3 -> 4.4
solution.description: Write the first set of statistics down in shorthand; the passage carries more than three numbers, so keeping them straight on paper is necessary.

solution.operation: Map the France numbers over the same time frame: France GDP 4, vote share 4.3 dropped to 3.8
solution.result: France: GDP about 4 percent; vote share 4.3 -> 3.8
solution.description: Record the parallel statistics for the second country so the two can be compared directly.

solution.operation: State the goal: find something that must be true given only this information, and note the overall comparison
solution.result: China has a larger GDP share than France; China used to have a lower voting share than France but now has a higher one
solution.description: Fix the standard (must be true) and the one comparison the mapped numbers actually establish, before reading the choices.

solution.operation: Test (A): does China's 2010 voting-share increase prove its earlier GDP was under 10 percent?
solution.result: Eliminated: the passage never says voting share is based on GDP, so this does not have to be true
solution.description: Reject the choice that requires an unstated causal link between voting share and GDP.

solution.operation: Test (B) against the mapped numbers: under direct proportionality, twice the GDP would mean twice the voting share
solution.result: Kept: China's GDP is more than twice France's while their voting shares are almost the same, so the shares are not directly proportional
solution.description: Check the choice arithmetically against the recorded figures; the mismatch it describes is visible in the passage's own numbers.

solution.operation: Test (C): does the passage report a rate of change in either country's GDP share?
solution.result: Eliminated: China's share is higher now, but nothing says whether France's share is rising or how fast
solution.description: Reject the comparison of growth rates, since the passage gives only single-time-frame GDP levels.

solution.operation: Test (D): does the passage support a claim about the Chinese government's satisfaction?
solution.result: Eliminated: there is no way to know this, nor whether a move from about 3 percent to 4.4 percent counts as small or large
solution.description: Reject the choice that adds an attitude no sentence in the passage reports.

solution.operation: Test (E): does the passage state how the voting-share figures were determined?
solution.result: Eliminated: this could be speculated but cannot be proven from the information given
solution.description: Reject the plausible-sounding explanation, since an inference must be provable from the passage, not merely possible.

key_reminders: An Inference answer must be provable from the passage alone, not merely plausible.
When a passage carries more than three numbers, map them on paper before reading the choices.
Directly proportional means a country with twice the GDP would have twice the voting share.
common_mistakes: Assuming World Bank voting share is set by GDP, which makes (A) and (E) look provable when the passage never links them.
Reading China's higher current GDP share as evidence about the rate of change in (C), though only one time frame's levels are given.

concept.technique_name: cube root extraction by digit-by-digit determination

examples.problem_statement: Using the Cube Root Extraction Algorithm technique: A manual algorithm for extracting cube roots of large integers through digit-by-digit determination using grouping, reference tables, and subtraction operations. Given: example 1 number = 84604519; example 1 cube root = 439; example 1 L = 4; example 1 M = 3; example 1 R = 9; example 1 R^3 = 729; example 1 3R^2M = 243M; example 2 number = 279726264. Reproduce the method step by step and state the final result.

solution.operation: Group the number into three-digit segments from right to left
solution.result: The number of groups gives the number of digits in the cube root
solution.description: Partition the digits into threes from the right; each group of three digits contributes exactly one digit to the cube root.

solution.operation: Read the unit digit of the original number into Table 1 to obtain the unit digit R of the cube root
solution.result: The rightmost digit R of the cube root is fixed
solution.description: Use the table lookup because a cube's last digit determines its root's last digit uniquely, so R needs no trial.

solution.operation: Find in Table 2 the largest cube that is less than the leftmost group
solution.result: The leftmost digit L of the cube root is fixed
solution.description: Bound the leading group from below by a perfect cube; the root of that cube is the leading digit L.

solution.operation: Subtract R^3 from the original number and ignore the last zero digit of the result
solution.result: A reduced number carrying the information about the remaining middle digit
solution.description: Strip out the contribution already accounted for by R, then drop the trailing zero the subtraction leaves behind.

solution.operation: Form 3R^2M and choose M so that the unit digit of 3R^2M matches the relevant digit of the subtraction result
solution.result: The middle digit M of the cube root is fixed
solution.description: Match unit digits in the expression 3R^2M, which is the term that carries M into that digit position, to pin M down.

solution.operation: Write L, M and R side by side in that order
solution.result: The complete cube root
solution.description: Assemble the digits found in steps 2, 3 and 5 into their place-value positions to state the final root.

examples.answer: Example 5: Cube root of 84604519 = 439; Example 6: Cube root of 279726264 has R=4 (incomplete solution in this chunk)

key_reminders: Group digits in threes from the right: one group yields one digit of the cube root.
The unit digit of a perfect cube determines the unit digit R of its root uniquely (Table 1).
The leading digit L comes from the largest cube below the leftmost group (Table 2).
common_mistakes: Grouping the digits in threes from the left instead of from the right, which misplaces the leading group and so gives the wrong L.
Forgetting to drop the trailing zero after subtracting R^3, which shifts the digit compared against 3R^2M and yields the wrong M.
